title: ansible-live: watch a running playbook from a Claude Code pane
description:
## Goal

ansible-live: watch a running `ansible-playbook` from inside Claude Code. An Ansible callback
plugin records each run as it happens; a Claude Code plugin (a mod) draws it in a pane: playbook
and play, the task in progress, a host × task grid of outcomes, and the latest failure's message.
Any playbook, any inventory, started from Claude or from any other terminal. Published on GitHub
as `igouss/ansible-live` under MIT: the callback as the Galaxy collection `igouss.ansible_live`
(callback `igouss.ansible_live.live`, installable from the git URL before any Galaxy upload); the mod
through the repo itself acting as a Claude Code plugin marketplace
(`/plugin marketplace add igouss/ansible-live`).

## Shape

- One repo, laid out by capability: the event contract, the recorder (Ansible side), the viewer
  (Claude Code side).
- The contract is the only coupling between the two sides; both are tested against it.
- It is stream processing: the recorder appends events to an append-only log, which is the stream
  and keeps runs nobody was watching; the viewer follows it through a child process
  (`$.process.spawn` streams a child's output piece by piece) and folds each event as it arrives.
  A mod cannot listen on a socket, and a push with no listener would lose the run.
- Viewer: functional core (events → what the pane shows, pure) and an imperative shell (the
  follower process, drawing).
- `testbed/` is an Ansible project of this machine under several names plus an unreachable ghost,
  with playbooks for a clean run, failures (fail, ignored, rescued), an unreachable host, and a run
  of any length and pace; `just testbed` holds each to its exit code. Tests and the demo use it.

## Known constraints

- In the mod, `$.fs.read` refuses a file over 4 MiB and cannot read part of one; the viewer
  therefore never reads a log whole, it follows it.
- No live source can come from OpenTelemetry: the community.general.opentelemetry callback builds
  its spans at `v2_playbook_on_stats`, and OTLP only exports ended spans.
- A run can die without `v2_playbook_on_stats` (Ctrl-C, SIGKILL); the viewer must not show it as
  running forever.

## Operator decision

2026-09-28, Iouri:

- "let's plan this as a reusable project that I can publish on github"
- Name: "ansible-live". License: "MIT".
- Viewers: "Claude Code pane only (Recommended)" — no standalone CLI viewer.
- The infra2 runs.sqlite live-recording change: "Drop it (Recommended)" — infra2 adopts this
  project's callback instead; runs.sqlite stays a record written when a run ends.
- Pane content chosen earlier the same day: "Pane" (not a status-line entry, not a finish toast).
- "ok, no OTEL. Why would mod read a file, this is more of a stream processing task. My current gh
  account. I'm not familiar with Galaxy, marketplace, make a decision for me. Create a ansoble
  project that ansible-live can test code on, we will install it on infra2 once the code is done."
  Decided for the operator on that authority: GitHub `igouss/ansible-live`; Galaxy namespace
  `igouss`, collection `ansible_live`; the repo is its own plugin marketplace. infra2 installs it
  once the code is done.

- "skip Galaxy upload until the code is ready, let's prove that this works before we start
  thinking about publishing. Let's start." Publishing (bead .6) waits until the pane is proven on
  real runs.

This approves: the project's name, license, scope (pane only), the publishing targets above, and
the testbed. Nothing else is approved. Still the operator's: every push, Galaxy upload and
listing (each is outward-facing), and the infra2 change that installs it.

title: Event contract v1 between recorder and viewer
description:
## What

Version 1 of the event contract between recorder and viewer, as a machine-checkable schema plus a
short spec in the repo.

It must settle:
- where a run's records live (default under `$XDG_STATE_HOME`, overridable by the operator) and how
  the viewer finds the run in progress and the recent ones; two runs at once are both findable;
- the events and their fields: run start (playbook, check mode, limit, extra-var names only,
  inventory hosts where known), play start, task start (incl. handlers), per-host result
  (ok/changed/failed/ignored/skipped/unreachable, message), run end with outcome;
- what the viewer concludes about a run that stopped without an end event (killed, interrupted);
- how a follower picks up the stream: from a run's start or from now, across several runs and two
  at once, with no event lost or seen twice while the recorder writes; how old logs are pruned;
- how the schema version is stated and what a reader does with a version it does not know;
- that task arguments and result dumps are never recorded (secrets); messages are bounded.

## Acceptance

- Schema file and spec committed; examples of every event validate; a malformed example is
  rejected by the schema (seen red).
- Each point above is answered in the spec or recorded as a flagged assumption on this bead.
close_reason: Spec, schemas, check.py, examples and TLA+ model committed in 7c7b301; every acceptance point proven (see comments).

title: Recorder: Ansible callback writing the contract as a run happens
description:
## What

The Ansible callback plugin, shipped in a Galaxy collection, that records every run per the
contract as it happens. Enabled with `callbacks_enabled`; aggregate type, so it runs beside any
stdout callback. Honours check mode and `--limit`; costs a playbook no noticeable time.

## Acceptance

- Unit tests (pytest) drive the callback through a run's callbacks with Ansible stand-ins and
  assert the records written, each expected value spelled out; interrupted run covered.
- Property tests (Hypothesis): every record written validates against the contract schema.
- A real `ansible-playbook` against localhost produces records that validate.
- mutmut over the recorder; surviving mutants killed or argued equivalent on this bead.
- Overhead measured on a run of a few hundred task results; the number recorded here.

title: Viewer core: events to pane model, pure
description:
## What

The viewer's functional core, in TypeScript and free of Claude Code APIs: from a run's events (in
contract form, possibly a truncated prefix, possibly of an unknown later version) to the pane's
model — playbook, play, task in progress, host × task grid of outcomes, counts, the latest failure
message, and whether the run is running, ended (with outcome) or presumed dead.

## Acceptance

- Property tests with Hegel (TypeScript): e.g. a prefix of a run never shows a later task; counts
  equal the results folded; any valid event sequence folds without throwing.
- Unit tests for zero, one and many hosts/tasks.
- Stryker over the core; survivors killed or argued equivalent on this bead.

title: Viewer pane: the Claude Code plugin
description:
## What

The Claude Code plugin: a pane that shows the run in progress (else the latest run) through the
core, fed by following the event stream while the pane is open; no follower runs while it is
closed. A slash command
opens it; the operator can pick an earlier or a concurrent run. Works on the terminal and desktop
surfaces and at narrow widths. Records location per the contract, overridable in plugin options.

## Acceptance

- `claude plugin validate` clean; `claude plugin test` mounts the pane on `terminal` and `desktop`
  with fake runs: no run, one running, one ended failed, two concurrent.
- Seen live in a session while a real playbook runs (screenshot/GIF kept for the README).

title: Acceptance: Gherkin scenarios over a real playbook
description:
## What

Gherkin acceptance scenarios at the boundary: the `testbed/` playbooks run for real, with the
callback enabled, and what the pane shows during and after it. Covers: a clean run, a failed task,
an unreachable host, check mode, an interrupted run, two runs at once.

## Acceptance

- Scenarios run in CI and locally with one command; each was seen failing before it passed.

title: Publish: README, CI, release, marketplace
description:
## What

Everything a stranger needs to find, install and trust it: README (what it is, a GIF of the pane,
install for both halves, configuration, the contract), CHANGELOG, CONTRIBUTING; GitHub Actions
running every gate; release flow that builds the Galaxy collection and the marketplace entry from
one version; the plugin listed in a marketplace.

## Acceptance

- A fresh machine installs both halves from the published artifacts by following the README alone,
  and sees a run in the pane.
- Targets per the epic's operator decision; each push, upload and listing asked for before it
  happens.
